# Introduction

Modeling financial return series requires accounting for features that deviate from the assumptions of classical Gaussian models. Empirical returns often exhibit heavy tails, abrupt jumps, and periods of elevated volatility, reflecting the complex dynamics of real-world markets. These characteristics motivate the use of models that explicitly incorporate jump components, self-exciting event structures, or flexible distributional shapes.

In this project, we develop a simulation framework to study a discrete-time jump–diffusion model. These simulated datasets will later serve as controlled environments for evaluating different estimation approaches, including maximum likelihood estimation, the EM algorithm, and Bayesian methods.

We begin with the jump–diffusion model, which provides a simple but powerful extension of the Gaussian diffusion process by allowing returns to experience sudden, random jumps. This model forms the foundation for the more complex simulation settings considered in later sections.

# Jump–Diffusion Model and Simulation Setup

## Model specification
We consider a discrete-time jump–diffusion model for log-returns \(\{R_t\}_{t=1}^T\) of the form
\[
R_t = \mu + \sigma \varepsilon_t + Y_t Z_t,\quad t = 1,\dots,T,
\]
where
\[
\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1), \qquad
Y_t \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p), \qquad
Z_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_J, \sigma_J^2),
\]
and \(\varepsilon_t\), \(Y_t\), and \(Z_t\) are mutually independent across time. Here \(\mu\) is the drift, \(\sigma\) is the diffusion (continuous) volatility, \(p\) is the jump probability at each time step, and \(\mu_J, \sigma_J^2\) describe the distribution of jump sizes. In the simulation study below, we fix \(T = 2000\) and consider several parameter regimes (low-, medium-, and high-risk)

The following code simulates jump–diffusion returns under the three regimes and visualizes the resulting series.

## Theoretical background and link to estimation

The jump–diffusion specification
\[
R_t = \mu + \sigma \varepsilon_t + Y_t Z_t
\]
can be viewed as a finite mixture model for the marginal distribution of returns. Conditioning on whether a jump occurs at time \(t\),

- with probability \(1-p\), \(Y_t = 0\) and
  \[
  R_t \mid (Y_t = 0) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2),
  \]
- with probability \(p\), \(Y_t = 1\) and
  \[
  R_t \mid (Y_t = 1) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu + \mu_J,\, \sigma^2 + \sigma_J^2),
  \]
  because the diffusion shock \(\sigma \varepsilon_t\) and the jump \(Z_t\) add as independent Gaussian terms.

Marginally, the distribution of \(R_t\) is therefore a two-component Gaussian mixture,
\[
R_t \sim (1-p)\,\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)
\;+\;
p\,\mathcal{N}\bigl(\mu + \mu_J,\; \sigma^2 + \sigma_J^2\bigr),
\]
with parameters
\[
\theta = (\mu, \sigma, p, \mu_J, \sigma_J).
\]

In the simulation step above, we fixed \(\theta\) at three different values corresponding to low-, medium-, and high-risk regimes, thereby generating return series with increasingly frequent and severe jumps. These datasets serve as controlled environments in which the true parameter values are known by construction.

In the **estimation step**, we reverse the perspective: we now treat \(\theta\) as unknown and the simulated returns \(\{R_t\}\) as observed data. Using the Gaussian mixture representation of the jump–diffusion model, we construct the log-likelihood as a function of \(\theta\) and obtain parameter estimates via numerical maximization (maximum likelihood estimation).

##Frequentist Estimation (MLE and Bootstrap)

Recall that under the jump–diffusion specification,
\[
R_t = \mu + \sigma \varepsilon_t + Y_t Z_t,
\]
with
\[
\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1), \quad
Y_t \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p), \quad
Z_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_J, \sigma_J^2),
\]
the unconditional distribution of a single return \(R_t\) is a two-component Gaussian mixture:
\[
R_t \sim (1-p)\,\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)
\;+\;
p\,\mathcal{N}\bigl(\mu + \mu_J,\; \sigma^2 + \sigma_J^2\bigr),
\]
with parameter vector
\[
\theta = (\mu, \sigma, p, \mu_J, \sigma_J).
\]

For an observed series \(R_1,\dots,R_T\), the likelihood is
\[
L(\theta)
=
\prod_{t=1}^T 
\left[
(1-p)\,\phi(R_t; \mu, \sigma^2)
+
p\,\phi(R_t; \mu+\mu_J,\ \sigma^2 + \sigma_J^2)
\right],
\]
where \(\phi(\cdot; m, v)\) denotes the Gaussian density with mean \(m\) and variance \(v\). The log-likelihood is
\[
\ell(\theta)
=
\sum_{t=1}^T
\log\!\left[
(1-p)\,\phi(R_t; \mu, \sigma^2)
+
p\,\phi(R_t; \mu+\mu_J,\ \sigma^2 + \sigma_J^2)
\right].
\]

Because \(\sigma > 0\), \(\sigma_J > 0\), and \(0 < p < 1\) must hold, it is convenient to reparameterize the model in terms of an unconstrained parameter vector
\[
\phi = (\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi_3, \phi_4, \phi_5)
      = (\mu,\ \log\sigma,\ \text{logit}(p),\ \mu_J,\ \log\sigma_J),
\]
and define the mapping from \(\phi\) back to the original parameters,
\[
\sigma = e^{\phi_2}, \qquad
p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\phi_3}}, \qquad
\sigma_J = e^{\phi_5}.
\]
This guarantees \(\sigma > 0\), \(\sigma_J > 0\), and \(0 < p < 1\) for all \(\phi \in \mathbb{R}^5\), so that the optimizer only explores feasible parameter values.

In practice, the log-likelihood is evaluated in a numerically stable way using a log-sum-exp formulation. For each time point \(t\), define
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log f_1(R_t) &= \log\!\bigl(\phi(R_t; \mu, \sigma^2)\bigr),\\
\log f_2(R_t) &= \log\!\bigl(\phi(R_t; \mu+\mu_J,\ \sigma^2 + \sigma_J^2)\bigr),
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\log w_1 = \log(1-p), \qquad \log w_2 = \log(p).
\]
Then
\[
\log\!\left[(1-p)\,f_1(R_t) + p\,f_2(R_t)\right]
=
\log\!\left[e^{\log w_1 + \log f_1(R_t)} + e^{\log w_2 + \log f_2(R_t)}\right]
\]
is computed via
\[
m_t = \max\{\log w_1 + \log f_1(R_t),\ \log w_2 + \log f_2(R_t)\},
\]
\[
\log\!\left[(1-p)\,f_1(R_t) + p\,f_2(R_t)\right]
=
m_t + \log\!\left(
e^{\log w_1 + \log f_1(R_t) - m_t}
+
e^{\log w_2 + \log f_2(R_t) - m_t}
\right),
\]
and the total log-likelihood is obtained by summing over \(t\).

The maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) is defined as
\[
\hat{\phi}
=
\arg\max_{\phi \in \mathbb{R}^5} \ \ell\bigl(\theta(\phi)\bigr), 
\qquad
\hat{\theta} = \theta(\hat{\phi}),
\]
where \(\theta(\phi)\) denotes the transformation from \(\phi\) to \((\mu, \sigma, p, \mu_J, \sigma_J)\). In the implementation below, this optimization problem is solved numerically using the BFGS quasi-Newton method applied to the negative log-likelihood in \(\phi\)-space. Two safeguards are used. The returns are first rescaled to unit standard deviation, so that the optimizer works with numbers of order one, and the estimates are transformed back afterwards. The optimizer is then started from several points (four initial jump probabilities and two initial jump sizes) and the best maximum is kept, because the mixture likelihood has local maxima, including one in which the "jump" component describes ordinary days.


```{r jd-simulated-data}
# Simulation of jump–diffusion returns under three regimes

set.seed(12345)  # reproducibility

# Jump–diffusion simulator: R_t = mu + sigma * eps_t + Y_t * Z_t
simulate_jump_diffusion <- function(n_obs, mu, sigma, p, mu_J, sigma_J) {
  Y   <- rbinom(n_obs, size = 1, prob = p)       # jump indicators
  Z   <- rnorm(n_obs, mean = mu_J, sd = sigma_J) # jump sizes
  eps <- rnorm(n_obs, mean = 0, sd = 1)          # diffusion shocks
  R   <- mu + sigma * eps + Y * Z                # log-returns
  list(R = R, Y = Y, Z = Z)
}

# Length of each simulated series
n_obs <- 2000

# Parameter settings for three regimes
jd_params <- list(
  low = list(
    mu      = 0.0003,
    sigma   = 0.007,
    p       = 0.01,
    mu_J    = -0.015,
    sigma_J = 0.01
  ),
  medium = list(
    mu      = 0.0005,
    sigma   = 0.01,
    p       = 0.02,
    mu_J    = -0.03,
    sigma_J = 0.02
  ),
  high = list(
    mu      = 0.0000,
    sigma   = 0.02,
    p       = 0.06,
    mu_J    = -0.06,
    sigma_J = 0.04
  )
)

# Simulate data for each regime
sim_jd <- lapply(jd_params, function(par) {
  simulate_jump_diffusion(
    n_obs  = n_obs,
    mu     = par$mu,
    sigma  = par$sigma,
    p      = par$p,
    mu_J   = par$mu_J,
    sigma_J = par$sigma_J
  )
})

# Convenient aliases for later use
R_low    <- sim_jd$low$R
Y_low    <- sim_jd$low$Y

R_medium <- sim_jd$medium$R
Y_medium <- sim_jd$medium$Y

R_high   <- sim_jd$high$R
Y_high   <- sim_jd$high$Y
```

```{r jd-plots, fig.height=7}
par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(3, 4, 3, 1))

# Low risk
plot(R_low, type = "h",
     main = "Low-Risk Jump–Diffusion Returns",
     xlab = "", ylab = "R")
abline(h = 0, col = "gray")
points(which(Y_low == 1), R_low[Y_low == 1], col = "red", pch = 19)

# Medium risk
plot(R_medium, type = "h",
     main = "Medium-Risk Jump–Diffusion Returns",
     xlab = "", ylab = "R")
abline(h = 0, col = "gray")
points(which(Y_medium == 1), R_medium[Y_medium == 1], col = "red", pch = 19)

# High risk
plot(R_high, type = "h",
     main = "High-Risk Jump–Diffusion Returns",
     xlab = "Time", ylab = "R")
abline(h = 0, col = "gray")
points(which(Y_high == 1), R_high[Y_high == 1], col = "red", pch = 19)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

hist(R_low,    breaks = 40, main = "Low risk",    xlab = "R", freq = FALSE)
hist(R_medium, breaks = 40, main = "Medium risk", xlab = "R", freq = FALSE)
hist(R_high,   breaks = 40, main = "High risk",   xlab = "R", freq = FALSE)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The figures above illustrate the increasing frequency and magnitude of jumps as we move from the low- to the high-risk regime. The low-risk regime exhibits relatively stable returns with infrequent jumps, while the high-risk regime shows frequent, larger-magnitude discontinuities, consistent with the underlying parameter settings.

```{r mle-jd}
## ================================================
## MLE for jump–diffusion model (point estimates)
## ================================================

## 1. Transform phi -> theta
##    phi   = (mu, log_sigma, logit_p, mu_J, log_sigma_J)
##    theta = (mu, sigma, p, mu_J, sigma_J)

theta_from_phi <- function(phi) {
  mu          <- phi[1]
  log_sigma   <- phi[2]
  logit_p     <- phi[3]
  mu_J        <- phi[4]
  log_sigma_J <- phi[5]
  
  sigma_raw   <- exp(log_sigma)
  p_raw       <- 1 / (1 + exp(-logit_p))
  sigmaJ_raw  <- exp(log_sigma_J)
  
  # Clamp to safe ranges
  sigma   <- max(sigma_raw, 1e-6)
  sigma_J <- max(sigmaJ_raw, 1e-6)
  p       <- min(max(p_raw, 1e-6), 1 - 1e-6)
  
  theta <- c(mu, sigma, p, mu_J, sigma_J)
  names(theta) <- c("mu", "sigma", "p", "mu_J", "sigma_J")
  theta
}

## 2. Log-likelihood on theta-scale

loglik_jd_theta <- function(theta, R) {
  # ensure correct ordering
  theta <- theta[c("mu", "sigma", "p", "mu_J", "sigma_J")]
  mu      <- theta["mu"]
  sigma   <- theta["sigma"]
  p       <- theta["p"]
  mu_J    <- theta["mu_J"]
  sigma_J <- theta["sigma_J"]
  
  if (any(!is.finite(c(mu, sigma, p, mu_J, sigma_J)))) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  
  # No-jump: N(mu, sigma^2)
  log_f1 <- dnorm(R, mean = mu, sd = sigma, log = TRUE)
  
  # Jump: N(mu + mu_J, sigma^2 + sigma_J^2)
  sd2    <- sqrt(sigma^2 + sigma_J^2)
  log_f2 <- dnorm(R, mean = mu + mu_J, sd = sd2, log = TRUE)
  
  # Mixture log-density via log-sum-exp
  log_w1 <- log1p(-p)  # log(1 - p)
  log_w2 <- log(p)     # log(p)
  
  a <- log_w1 + log_f1
  b <- log_w2 + log_f2
  
  m       <- pmax(a, b)
  log_mix <- m + log(exp(a - m) + exp(b - m))
  
  sum(log_mix)
}

## 3. Negative log-likelihood in phi-space (for optim)

neg_loglik_jd_phi <- function(phi, R) {
  theta <- theta_from_phi(phi)
  ll    <- loglik_jd_theta(theta, R)
  if (!is.finite(ll)) return(1e12)
  -ll
}

## 4. Starting values

init_phi_jd <- function(R) {
  R_mean <- mean(R, na.rm = TRUE)
  R_sd   <- sd(R,   na.rm = TRUE)
  
  mu_init      <- R_mean
  sigma_init   <- ifelse(is.finite(R_sd) && R_sd > 0, R_sd / 2, 0.01)
  p_init       <- 0.05
  mu_J_init    <- -0.03
  sigma_J_init <- sigma_init
  
  c(
    mu          = mu_init,
    log_sigma   = log(sigma_init),
    logit_p     = qlogis(p_init),
    mu_J        = mu_J_init,
    log_sigma_J = log(sigma_J_init)
  )
}

## 5. Fit function – returns theta-hat (with names) and convergence info
##    Returns are rescaled to unit sd and BFGS is started from several points;
##    the best maximum is kept (the mixture likelihood has local maxima).

multi_starts_jd <- function(x) {
  starts <- list()
  for (p0 in c(0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1)) for (m0 in c(-1, -3)) {
    starts[[length(starts) + 1]] <- c(mu = mean(x), log_sigma = log(0.8), logit_p = qlogis(p0),
                                      mu_J = m0, log_sigma_J = log(2))
  }
  starts
}

fit_jd_mle_simple <- function(R, init_phi = NULL, control = list()) {
  s_R <- sd(R)
  x   <- R / s_R                                   # rescaled returns
  starts <- if (is.null(init_phi)) multi_starts_jd(x) else list(init_phi)

  best <- NULL
  for (phi0 in starts) {
    opt <- optim(
      par     = phi0,
      fn      = neg_loglik_jd_phi,
      R       = x,
      method  = "BFGS",
      control = modifyList(list(maxit = 2000, reltol = 1e-12), control)
    )
    if (is.null(best) || opt$value < best$value) best <- opt
  }

  theta_hat <- theta_from_phi(best$par)
  # Undo the rescaling (p is unaffected)
  scale_pars <- c("mu", "sigma", "mu_J", "sigma_J")
  theta_hat[scale_pars] <- theta_hat[scale_pars] * s_R
  # Make sure we ALWAYS have the standard names in the standard order
  theta_hat <- theta_hat[c("mu", "sigma", "p", "mu_J", "sigma_J")]

  list(
    par_theta   = theta_hat,
    logLik      = loglik_jd_theta(theta_hat, R),
    convergence = best$convergence,
    message     = best$message
  )
}

## 6. Fit for all regimes (using your existing sim_jd and jd_params)

regimes <- c("low", "medium", "high")

fit_list <- lapply(regimes, function(reg) {
  R_reg <- sim_jd[[reg]]$R
  fit_jd_mle_simple(R_reg)
})
names(fit_list) <- regimes

## Quick sanity check: are mus finite?
sapply(fit_list, function(x) x$par_theta["mu"])

## 7. Build summary table: true values vs estimates

param_names <- c("mu", "sigma", "p", "mu_J", "sigma_J")

summary_table <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(regimes, function(reg) {
    true_par  <- jd_params[[reg]]
    est_theta <- fit_list[[reg]]$par_theta
    
    # true_par is a list; extract in same order as param_names
    true_vec <- unlist(true_par)[param_names]
    
    data.frame(
      regime     = reg,
      parameter  = param_names,
      true_value = true_vec,
      estimate   = round(as.numeric(est_theta[param_names]),4),
      row.names  = NULL
    )
  })
)

summary_table
```

The maximum likelihood estimates obtained from the simulated jump-diffusion datasets exhibit a clear relationship between parameter recovery and the frequency of jumps across regimes. In the medium- and high-risk settings, where jumps occur more frequently, the MLE performs reliably and recovers the true parameters with good accuracy: the drift $\mu$ and diffusion volatility $\sigma$ are estimated precisely, and the jump parameters $(p, \mu_J, \sigma_J)$ are close to their true values. In contrast, the low-risk regime, which contains very few jump events by construction, presents substantial challenges for estimation. While the continuous parameters $(\mu, \sigma)$ remain well identified, the jump-related parameters are poorly determined. On this dataset, which contains only 16 jumps, the estimated jump probability $p$ happens to be close to its true value, but the jump-size standard deviation $\sigma_J$ collapses to zero, and the bootstrap below shows that the estimate of $p$ is extremely uncertain. This pattern is consistent with the well-known difficulty of identifying mixture components when the mixing weight is extremely small. Overall, these results highlight that the MLE behaves appropriately when sufficient jump information is available but becomes unreliable in regimes with sparse jump activity.

In many statistical models, analytic expressions for the variance of an estimator
are difficult to obtain, either because the likelihood is complex, the
information matrix is unstable, or the estimator does not arise from closed-form
optimization. A general and widely applicable alternative is the nonparametric
bootstrap, which approximates the sampling distribution of an estimator by
repeated resampling of the observed data.

Let $\hat{\theta}$ denote an estimator of a parameter vector
$\theta = (\theta_1,\dots,\theta_d)$ based on an observed sample
$R = (R_1,\dots,R_T)$. The bootstrap procedure proceeds as follows:

1. Generate $B$ bootstrap samples $R^{*(1)},\dots,R^{*(B)}$ by sampling with
   replacement from the original data $\{R_t\}_{t=1}^T$.

2. For each bootstrap sample $R^{*(b)}$, compute the estimator
   $\hat{\theta}^{*(b)}$ using the same estimation algorithm applied to the
   original data. The bootstrap replicates
   \[
   \hat{\theta}^{*(1)},\dots,\hat{\theta}^{*(B)}
   \]
   provide an empirical approximation to the sampling distribution of
   $\hat{\theta}$.

3. For each component $\theta_j$, the bootstrap estimate of the standard error is
   \[
   \widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_{\mathrm{boot}}(\hat{\theta}_j)
   =
   \sqrt{
     \frac{1}{B-1}
     \sum_{b=1}^B
     \bigl(\hat{\theta}^{*(b)}_j - \bar{\theta}^*_j\bigr)^2
   },
   \]
   where
   \[
   \bar{\theta}^*_j = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \hat{\theta}^{*(b)}_j
   \]
   is the bootstrap mean.

The bootstrap standard error therefore captures the finite-sample variability of
the estimator \emph{regardless of the method used to compute it}. This feature
makes bootstrap inference particularly valuable for models such as finite
mixtures or latent-variable models, where the Hessian may be singular or
difficult to compute, or for estimation methods such as the EM algorithm or
Bayesian posterior modes, where no closed-form variance expression is available.

By consistently applying the same estimation procedure to each resampled dataset,
the bootstrap provides a unified and model-agnostic measure of estimator
uncertainty that can be compared across different estimation methods.

```{r se-mle-jd-bootstrap, message=FALSE}
## ================================================
## Bootstrap SEs for the jump–diffusion MLE
## ================================================

# Assumes the following are already defined from previous chunks:
# - jd_params   (list of true parameters for low/medium/high)
# - sim_jd      (simulated data for each regime)
# - regimes     <- c("low", "medium", "high")
# - fit_jd_mle_simple(R, ...)  (returns par_theta with names)

bootstrap_jd <- function(R, B = 300, control = list()) {
  param_names <- c("mu", "sigma", "p", "mu_J", "sigma_J")
  est_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = B, ncol = length(param_names))
  colnames(est_mat) <- param_names
  
  n_success <- 0L
  
  for (b in seq_len(B)) {
    # Resample returns with replacement
    R_b <- sample(R, size = length(R), replace = TRUE)
    
    # Try to fit the model on the bootstrap sample
    fit_b <- try(fit_jd_mle_simple(R_b, control = control), silent = TRUE)
    
    # Skip failed fits or non-list results
    if (inherits(fit_b, "try-error") || !is.list(fit_b)) next
    
    # If fit_jd_mle_simple includes convergence info, you can optionally skip
    # non-converged fits; here we just check if such a field exists:
    if (!is.null(fit_b$convergence) && fit_b$convergence != 0) next
    
    est_b <- fit_b$par_theta[param_names]
    if (any(!is.finite(est_b))) next
    
    n_success <- n_success + 1L
    est_mat[n_success, ] <- est_b
  }
  
  if (n_success == 0L) {
    stop("All bootstrap fits failed for this series.")
  }
  
  # Keep only successful rows
  est_mat <- est_mat[seq_len(n_success), , drop = FALSE]
  
  boot_mean <- colMeans(est_mat, na.rm = TRUE)
  boot_se   <- apply(est_mat, 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  list(
    estimates = est_mat,
    mean      = boot_mean,
    se        = boot_se,
    n_success = n_success
  )
}

## Run bootstrap for each regime
set.seed(123)  # for reproducibility of bootstrap resamples

boot_list <- lapply(regimes, function(reg) {
  R_reg <- sim_jd[[reg]]$R
  bootstrap_jd(R_reg, B = 300)
})
names(boot_list) <- regimes

## Build summary table: true values, MLE estimates, bootstrap SEs

param_names <- c("mu", "sigma", "p", "mu_J", "sigma_J")

summary_boot <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(regimes, function(reg) {
    true_par  <- jd_params[[reg]]
    mle_theta <- fit_list[[reg]]$par_theta
    boot_se   <- boot_list[[reg]]$se
    
    data.frame(
      regime     = reg,
      parameter  = param_names,
      true_value = unlist(true_par)[param_names],
      mle_est    = round(as.numeric(mle_theta[param_names]), 4),
      boot_se    = round(as.numeric(boot_se[param_names]), 4),
      row.names  = NULL
    )
  })
)

summary_boot
```

The nonparametric bootstrap standard errors reinforce the identifiability patterns observed in the point estimates. In the medium- and high-risk regimes, where jump events occur with reasonable frequency, the bootstrap distribution yields stable and interpretable uncertainty measures for all parameters. However, in the low-risk regime, the bootstrap results deteriorate sharply. Because many bootstrap resamples contain few or no jumps, the likelihood surface becomes effectively flat in the jump parameters, resulting in very large standard errors for the jump parameters; the standard error of $p$ is more than thirty times the estimate itself. This behavior does not reflect numerical issues but instead arises from fundamental non-identifiability of the jump component when the probability of observing a jump is very small. The bootstrap analysis therefore confirms that reliable inference for jump parameters requires a sufficient number of jump observations, while the diffusion parameters $(\mu, \sigma)$ remain consistently estimable across all regimes.

The theoretical formulation of the jump-diffusion likelihood corresponds exactly to the estimation procedure implemented in the accompanying code. The mixture representation of the return distribution,
\[
R_t \sim (1-p)\,\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)+p\,\mathcal{N}(\mu+\mu_J,\sigma^2+\sigma_J^2),
\]
is the basis for the log-likelihood function evaluated in the optimizer. The reparameterization
\[
(\mu,\log\sigma,\mathrm{logit}(p),\mu_J,\log\sigma_J)
\]
ensures that the constraints $\sigma>0$, $\sigma_J>0$, and $0<p<1$ are automatically enforced throughout the numerical search, precisely as described in the theoretical section. Likewise, the log-sum-exp formulation used in the code mirrors the stabilized likelihood expression derived algebraically. Thus, the implemented MLE routine is a direct computational translation of the model assumptions and likelihood structure presented in the theory.

##EM Estimation and Bootstrap

The jump-diffusion specification
\[
R_t = \mu + \sigma \varepsilon_t + Y_t Z_t,\qquad t = 1,\dots,T,
\]
with
\[
\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1), \quad
Y_t \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p), \quad
Z_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_J,\sigma_J^2),
\]
implies that the unconditional distribution of each return \(R_t\) is a
two-component Gaussian mixture. Conditional on the latent jump
indicator \(Y_t\),
\[
R_t \mid (Y_t = 0) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2), \qquad
R_t \mid (Y_t = 1) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu + \mu_J,\ \sigma^2 + \sigma_J^2),
\]
so that
\[
R_t \sim (1-p)\,\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)
\;+\;
p\,\mathcal{N}\!\bigl(\mu+\mu_J,\ \sigma^2+\sigma_J^2\bigr),
\]
with parameter vector
\[
\theta = (\mu,\sigma,p,\mu_J,\sigma_J).
\]

Direct maximization of the mixture likelihood can be numerically
challenging, especially when the jump probability \(p\) is small.
Instead, we exploit the latent-variable representation and use the
expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm to obtain the maximum
likelihood estimate of \(\theta\).

\paragraph{Complete-data formulation.}
Introduce latent indicators
\[
Y_t =
\begin{cases}
0, & \text{if no jump occurs at time } t,\\[3pt]
1, & \text{if a jump occurs at time } t,
\end{cases}
\]
together with the latent jump sizes \(Z_t\), and define the complete data
as \(\{(R_t,Y_t,Z_t)\}_{t=1}^T\). Treating the jump size as missing data,
and not only the indicator, is what keeps the constraint that the jump
component's variance is \(\sigma^2+\sigma_J^2\): given the latent
variables, \(R_t-\mu-Y_tZ_t\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)\) and
\(Z_t\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_J,\sigma_J^2)\), so the complete-data
log-likelihood is, up to a constant,
\[
\ell_c(\theta)
=
\sum_{t=1}^T\Bigl[
Y_t\log p+(1-Y_t)\log(1-p)
-\tfrac12\log\sigma^2-\frac{(R_t-\mu-Y_tZ_t)^2}{2\sigma^2}
+Y_t\Bigl\{-\tfrac12\log\sigma_J^2-\frac{(Z_t-\mu_J)^2}{2\sigma_J^2}\Bigr\}
\Bigr].
\]

\paragraph{E-step.}
Given a current parameter value \(\theta^{(k)}\), the E-step computes
\[
Q(\theta \mid \theta^{(k)})
=
\mathbb{E}_{\theta^{(k)}}\bigl[\ell_c(\theta)\,\big|\{R_t\}_{t=1}^T\bigr].
\]
This requires the posterior jump probabilities
\[
\tau_t^{(k)}
=
\Pr_{\theta^{(k)}}(Y_t = 1 \mid R_t)
=
\frac{
p^{(k)}\,\phi\!\bigl(R_t;\mu^{(k)}+\mu_J^{(k)},\ (\sigma^{(k)})^2 + (\sigma_J^{(k)})^2\bigr)
}{
(1-p^{(k)})\,\phi\!\bigl(R_t;\mu^{(k)},(\sigma^{(k)})^2\bigr)
+
p^{(k)}\,\phi\!\bigl(R_t;\mu^{(k)}+\mu_J^{(k)},\ (\sigma^{(k)})^2 + (\sigma_J^{(k)})^2\bigr)
},
\]
and the moments of the jump size on jump days. Since
\(R_t-\mu=Z_t+\sigma\varepsilon_t\) when \(Y_t=1\),
\[
Z_t\mid R_t,\,Y_t=1\ \sim\ \mathcal{N}(m_t,v),\qquad
m_t=\mu_J+\frac{\sigma_J^2}{\sigma^2+\sigma_J^2}\,(R_t-\mu-\mu_J),\qquad
v=\frac{\sigma^2\sigma_J^2}{\sigma^2+\sigma_J^2},
\]
evaluated at \(\theta^{(k)}\). Write \(a_t=\tau_t m_t=\mathbb{E}[Y_tZ_t\mid R_t]\) and
\(b_t=\tau_t(m_t^2+v)=\mathbb{E}[Y_tZ_t^2\mid R_t]\).

\paragraph{M-step.}
Maximizing \(Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(k)})\) gives closed-form updates:
\[
p^{(k+1)}=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\tau_t,\qquad
\mu^{(k+1)}=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T(R_t-a_t),
\]
\[
(\sigma^{(k+1)})^2=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\Bigl[(R_t-\mu^{(k+1)})^2-2(R_t-\mu^{(k+1)})\,a_t+b_t\Bigr],
\]
\[
\mu_J^{(k+1)}=\frac{\sum_t a_t}{\sum_t\tau_t},\qquad
(\sigma_J^{(k+1)})^2=\frac{\sum_t\bigl(b_t-2\mu_J^{(k+1)}a_t+\tau_t(\mu_J^{(k+1)})^2\bigr)}{\sum_t\tau_t}.
\]
Each iteration cannot decrease the observed-data log-likelihood.

\paragraph{Convergence.}
Starting from an initial guess \(\theta^{(0)}\), the EM algorithm
alternates between E-steps and M-steps until convergence, typically
assessed via the change in the log-likelihood or the change in
\(\theta^{(k)}\) between successive iterations. The resulting estimate
\(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{EM}}\) is a local maximizer of the
observed-data likelihood for the jump-diffusion mixture model. As for the
MLE, the algorithm is started from several initial values and the solution
with the highest log-likelihood is used as the EM-based point estimate of
the jump-diffusion parameters in each simulated regime.


```{r em-jd-bootstrap, message=FALSE}
## ================================================
## EM estimation for jump–diffusion model
## (latent jump indicators and jump sizes)
## ================================================

## 1. Exact EM for the jump-diffusion model
##    Latent data: jump indicators Y_t and jump sizes Z_t.
##    E-step: tau_t = P(Y_t = 1 | R_t), and Z_t | R_t, Y_t = 1 ~ N(m_t, v)
##    M-step: closed-form updates of (p, mu, sigma, mu_J, sigma_J)

fit_em_jd_single <- function(R, p_init = 0.05, mu_J_init_sd = -1,
                             max_iter = 5000, tol = 1e-10) {
  R <- as.numeric(R)
  R_sd <- sd(R)
  
  ## -- Initialization (simple, data-driven) --
  mu      <- mean(R)
  sigma   <- R_sd / 1.2
  p       <- p_init
  mu_J    <- mu_J_init_sd * R_sd
  sigma_J <- 2 * R_sd
  
  loglik_old <- -Inf
  for (iter in seq_len(max_iter)) {
    theta <- c(mu = mu, sigma = sigma, p = p, mu_J = mu_J, sigma_J = sigma_J)
    
    ## -- E-step: jump probabilities and jump-size moments --
    log_f0 <- log1p(-p) + dnorm(R, mu, sigma, log = TRUE)
    log_f1 <- log(p) + dnorm(R, mu + mu_J, sqrt(sigma^2 + sigma_J^2), log = TRUE)
    tau <- 1 / (1 + exp(log_f0 - log_f1))
    
    w   <- sigma_J^2 / (sigma^2 + sigma_J^2)
    m_t <- mu_J + w * (R - mu - mu_J)      # E[Z_t | R_t, Y_t = 1]
    v   <- sigma^2 * w                     # Var[Z_t | R_t, Y_t = 1]
    a_t <- tau * m_t                       # E[Y_t Z_t   | R_t]
    b_t <- tau * (m_t^2 + v)               # E[Y_t Z_t^2 | R_t]
    
    ## -- M-step --
    p       <- mean(tau)
    mu      <- mean(R - a_t)
    sigma   <- sqrt(mean((R - mu)^2 - 2 * (R - mu) * a_t + b_t))
    mu_J    <- sum(a_t) / sum(tau)
    sigma_J <- sqrt(max(sum(b_t - 2 * mu_J * a_t + tau * mu_J^2) / sum(tau), 1e-12))
    
    if (p < 1e-5 || sigma_J < 1e-7) break  # jump component has vanished
    
    ## -- Convergence check on the observed-data log-likelihood --
    loglik_new <- loglik_jd_theta(c(mu = mu, sigma = sigma, p = p, mu_J = mu_J, sigma_J = sigma_J), R)
    if (abs(loglik_new - loglik_old) < tol * (1 + abs(loglik_new))) break
    loglik_old <- loglik_new
  }
  
  theta_hat <- c(mu = mu, sigma = sigma, p = p, mu_J = mu_J, sigma_J = sigma_J)
  list(par_theta = theta_hat, logLik = loglik_jd_theta(theta_hat, R), iter = iter)
}

## 2. Run EM from several starting values and keep the best solution

fit_em_jd <- function(R, max_iter = 5000, tol = 1e-10) {
  best <- NULL
  for (p0 in c(0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1)) for (m0 in c(-1, -3)) {
    fit <- fit_em_jd_single(R, p_init = p0, mu_J_init_sd = m0, max_iter = max_iter, tol = tol)
    if (is.finite(fit$logLik) && (is.null(best) || fit$logLik > best$logLik)) best <- fit
  }
  best
}

## 4. Fit EM for each regime

regimes <- c("low", "medium", "high")

fit_em_list <- lapply(regimes, function(reg) {
  R_reg <- sim_jd[[reg]]$R
  fit_em_jd(R_reg)
})
names(fit_em_list) <- regimes

## Quick check of EM estimates
sapply(fit_em_list, function(x) x$par_theta)

## 5. Bootstrap SEs for EM estimator

bootstrap_em_jd <- function(R, B = 300, max_iter = 5000, tol = 1e-10) {
  param_names <- c("mu", "sigma", "p", "mu_J", "sigma_J")
  est_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = B, ncol = length(param_names))
  colnames(est_mat) <- param_names
  
  n_success <- 0L
  
  for (b in seq_len(B)) {
    R_b <- sample(R, size = length(R), replace = TRUE)
    
    fit_b <- try(fit_em_jd(R_b, max_iter = max_iter, tol = tol), silent = TRUE)
    if (inherits(fit_b, "try-error") || !is.list(fit_b)) next
    
    est_b <- fit_b$par_theta[param_names]
    if (any(!is.finite(est_b))) next
    
    n_success <- n_success + 1L
    est_mat[n_success, ] <- est_b
  }
  
  if (n_success == 0L) {
    stop("All EM bootstrap fits failed for this series.")
  }
  
  est_mat <- est_mat[seq_len(n_success), , drop = FALSE]
  
  boot_mean <- colMeans(est_mat, na.rm = TRUE)
  boot_se   <- apply(est_mat, 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  list(
    estimates = est_mat,
    mean      = boot_mean,
    se        = boot_se,
    n_success = n_success
  )
}

## 6. Run bootstrap for each regime

set.seed(456)  # separate seed from MLE bootstrap

boot_em_list <- lapply(regimes, function(reg) {
  R_reg <- sim_jd[[reg]]$R
  bootstrap_em_jd(R_reg, B = 300)
})
names(boot_em_list) <- regimes

## 7. Summary table: true values, EM estimates, bootstrap SEs

param_names <- c("mu", "sigma", "p", "mu_J", "sigma_J")

summary_em_boot <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(regimes, function(reg) {
    true_par <- jd_params[[reg]]
    em_theta <- fit_em_list[[reg]]$par_theta
    boot_se  <- boot_em_list[[reg]]$se
    
    data.frame(
      regime     = reg,
      parameter  = param_names,
      true_value = unlist(true_par)[param_names],
      em_est     = round(as.numeric(em_theta[param_names]), 4),
      boot_se    = round(as.numeric(boot_se[param_names]), 4),
      row.names  = NULL
    )
  })
)

summary_em_boot
```

The EM-based estimates for the jump-diffusion model display a pattern that closely parallels the behavior observed under maximum likelihood estimation, with performance strongly dependent on the frequency of jump events in the underlying regime. Because EM maximizes the same likelihood, its point estimates agree with the MLE to the reported precision. In the medium- and high-risk settings, where the data contain enough realizations from both mixture components, the EM algorithm accurately recovers the drift $\mu$, the diffusion volatility $\sigma$, and the jump parameters $(p, \mu_J, \sigma_J)$, with bootstrap standard errors that remain well-behaved across all parameters. In contrast, the low-risk regime poses a more challenging inference environment: as for the MLE, the jump-size standard deviation collapses toward zero and the bootstrap standard error of $p$ is many times larger than the estimate, reflecting the ambiguity created by the scarcity of observed jumps. Despite this, the EM algorithm still produces finite and interpretable estimates, and its bootstrap variability correctly reflects the increased uncertainty associated with the nearly unidentifiable jump component. Overall, the EM procedure offers a stable and computationally convenient alternative to direct likelihood maximization, particularly in moderate- and high-jump settings, while inheriting the same fundamental limitations when jump events are extremely rare.

## Bayesian Estimation via Gibbs Sampling

To complement the maximum likelihood and EM estimators, we employ a
Bayesian approach to infer the parameters of the jump-diffusion model
\[
R_t=\mu+\sigma\varepsilon_t+Y_t Z_t,
\qquad t=1,\ldots,T,
\]
where
\[
\varepsilon_t\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1),\quad
Y_t\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p),\quad
Z_t\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_J,\sigma_J^2).
\]
Marginally, each return follows the two–component Gaussian mixture
\[
R_t \sim (1-p)\,\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)
\;+\;
p\,\mathcal{N}(\mu+\mu_J,\ \sigma^2+\sigma_J^2).
\]
In the Bayesian formulation, the latent indicators \(Y_t\),
representing whether a jump occurred at time \(t\), are treated as
unobserved data. The Gibbs sampler exploits this latent–variable
representation to alternate between sampling the latent labels and
sampling the model parameters from their full conditional distributions.

### Latent–variable augmentation

Define
\[
Y_t =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if a jump occurs at time } t,\\
0, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]
and let \(\theta=(\mu,\sigma,p,\mu_J,\sigma_J)\) denote the parameter
vector. Augmenting only \(Y_t\) gives
\(R_t\mid (Y_t=1) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu+\mu_J,\ \sigma^2+\sigma_J^2)\), whose
variance mixes \(\sigma^2\) and \(\sigma_J^2\), so the variance updates are
not conjugate. We therefore also augment the jump sizes \(Z_t\). Given
both latent variables,
\[
R_t-\mu-Y_tZ_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),\qquad
Z_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_J,\sigma_J^2),
\]
which converts the mixture model into a conditionally Gaussian structure
with closed-form updates for every parameter.

### Priors
We adopt weakly informative priors chosen to stabilize estimation while
avoiding undue influence:
\[
p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a_0,b_0),\qquad
\mu,\mu_J \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\,\tau^2),
\]
\[
\sigma^2 \sim \mathrm{Inv{\text-}Gamma}(\alpha_0,\beta_0),\qquad
\sigma_J^2 \sim \mathrm{Inv{\text-}Gamma}(\gamma_0,\delta_0),
\]
with \(a_0=1\), \(b_0=9\), \(\tau=0.05\), \(\alpha_0=\gamma_0=2\) and
\(\beta_0=\delta_0=2\times10^{-4}\).
These priors ensure positivity of variances and allow the likelihood to
dominate the posterior in the medium– and high–jump regimes.

### Full conditional distributions

The Gibbs sampler cycles through the following updates.

#### 1. Sampling latent jump indicators and jump sizes
For each observation,
\[
\Pr(Y_t=1\mid R_t,\theta)
=
\frac{
p\,\phi\!\bigl(R_t;\mu+\mu_J,\ \sigma^2+\sigma_J^2\bigr)
}{
(1-p)\,\phi(R_t;\mu,\sigma^2)+
p\,\phi\!\bigl(R_t;\mu+\mu_J,\ \sigma^2+\sigma_J^2\bigr)
},
\]
and \(Y_t\) is drawn from a Bernoulli distribution with this probability.
On days with \(Y_t=1\) the jump size is drawn from
\[
Z_t\mid R_t,Y_t=1,\theta\ \sim\ \mathcal{N}\!\left(
\mu_J+\frac{\sigma_J^2}{\sigma^2+\sigma_J^2}(R_t-\mu-\mu_J),\ \
\frac{\sigma^2\sigma_J^2}{\sigma^2+\sigma_J^2}\right);
\]
on other days \(Z_t\) does not enter the likelihood and is set to zero.

#### 2. Updating the mixture weight \(p\)
Given the latent indicators, with \(N_1=\sum_t Y_t\),
\[
p\mid Y \sim \mathrm{Beta}\!\left(a_0+N_1,\quad b_0+T-N_1\right).
\]

#### 3. Updating the means
The drift uses all \(T\) observations after removing the sampled jumps,
and the jump mean uses the \(N_1\) sampled jump sizes:
\[
\mu \mid R,Y,Z,\sigma^2
\sim
\mathcal{N}\!\left(
\frac{\sigma^{-2}\sum_{t}(R_t-Y_tZ_t)}{\tau^{-2} + T \sigma^{-2}},
\quad
\frac{1}{\tau^{-2} + T \sigma^{-2}}
\right),
\]
\[
\mu_J \mid Y,Z,\sigma_J^2
\sim
\mathcal{N}\!\left(
\frac{\sigma_J^{-2} \sum_{t:Y_t=1}Z_t}
{\tau^{-2} + N_1 \sigma_J^{-2}},
\;
\frac{1}{\tau^{-2} + N_1\sigma_J^{-2}}
\right).
\]

#### 4. Updating variances
The diffusion and jump variances have inverse–Gamma full conditionals:
\[
\sigma^2 \mid R,Y,Z,\mu
\sim
\mathrm{Inv{\text-}Gamma}\!\left(
\alpha_0+\frac{T}{2},\quad
\beta_0+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t}(R_t-\mu-Y_tZ_t)^2
\right),
\]
\[
\sigma_J^2 \mid Y,Z,\mu_J
\sim
\mathrm{Inv{\text-}Gamma}\!\left(
\gamma_0+\frac{N_1}{2},\quad
\delta_0+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t:Y_t=1}(Z_t-\mu_J)^2
\right).
\]

### Gibbs sampling procedure

Starting from initial parameter values, the sampler iterates the following cycle:

1. Sample \(Y_t\), and \(Z_t\) on jump days, for all \(t\).
2. Sample \(p\) from its Beta conditional.
3. Sample \(\mu\) from its Gaussian conditional.
4. Sample \(\sigma^2\) from its inverse–Gamma conditional.
5. Sample \(\mu_J\) and then \(\sigma_J^2\) from their conditionals.

Each full Gibbs sweep produces a draw from the joint posterior
\[ p(\mu,\sigma,p,\mu_J,\sigma_J,Y,Z\mid R). \]
After discarding burn–in iterations and thinning if desired, the
remaining draws are used to compute posterior means, standard deviations,
and credible intervals for all parameters.

### Interpretation
The Gibbs sampler provides a fully Bayesian estimate of the jump–diffusion
parameters while naturally accounting for uncertainty in the latent jump
allocation. Unlike MLE and EM, which may struggle in low–jump regimes,
the Bayesian approach yields coherent posterior uncertainty
quantification that properly reflects identifiability limitations. In
settings with sufficient jump information, the posterior concentrates
around the true parameter values, closely matching the performance of
MLE and EM while providing richer inferential output.


```{r jd-gibbs}
## ================================================
## Gibbs sampler for jump–diffusion model
## (latent jump indicators and jump sizes)
## ================================================

## Inverse-Gamma sampler (shape = a, rate = b)
rinvgamma <- function(n, shape, rate) {
  1 / rgamma(n, shape = shape, rate = rate)
}

## One Gibbs run for a single return series R
## Latent variables: jump indicators Y_t and jump sizes Z_t
gibbs_jd <- function(R,
                     n_iter   = 10000,
                     burnin   = 2000,
                     thin     = 10,
                     hyper_p  = c(a = 1, b = 9),   # Beta prior for p
                     hyper_mv = list(
                       tau    = 0.05,   # prior sd for mu and mu_J
                       alpha0 = 2,      # Inv-Gamma shape (sigma^2 and sigma_J^2)
                       beta0  = 2e-4    # Inv-Gamma rate  (sigma^2 and sigma_J^2)
                     )) {
  R <- as.numeric(R)
  Tlen <- length(R)
  
  ## -- Priors --
  a_p    <- hyper_p["a"]
  b_p    <- hyper_p["b"]
  tau    <- hyper_mv$tau
  alpha0 <- hyper_mv$alpha0
  beta0  <- hyper_mv$beta0
  
  ## -- Storage for MCMC draws (JD parameters) --
  keep_idx <- seq(from = burnin + 1, to = n_iter, by = thin)
  n_keep   <- length(keep_idx)
  
  param_names <- c("mu", "sigma", "p", "mu_J", "sigma_J")
  draws <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_keep, ncol = length(param_names))
  colnames(draws) <- param_names
  
  ## -- Initialization (rough, data-based) --
  R_sd    <- sd(R)
  mu      <- mean(R)
  sigma2  <- (R_sd / 1.5)^2
  p       <- 0.05
  mu_J    <- -R_sd
  sigmaJ2 <- (2 * R_sd)^2
  
  iter_keep <- 0L
  
  for (iter in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    ## ============================
    ## 1. Sample jump indicators Y_t and jump sizes Z_t
    ## ============================
    log_f0 <- log1p(-p) + dnorm(R, mu, sqrt(sigma2), log = TRUE)
    log_f1 <- log(p) + dnorm(R, mu + mu_J, sqrt(sigma2 + sigmaJ2), log = TRUE)
    prob1  <- 1 / (1 + exp(log_f0 - log_f1))
    Y  <- rbinom(Tlen, size = 1, prob = prob1) == 1
    n1 <- sum(Y)
    
    Z <- numeric(Tlen)
    if (n1 > 0) {
      w <- sigmaJ2 / (sigma2 + sigmaJ2)
      Z[Y] <- rnorm(n1, mean = mu_J + w * (R[Y] - mu - mu_J), sd = sqrt(sigma2 * w))
    }
    
    ## ============================
    ## 2. Sample p | Y
    ## ============================
    p <- rbeta(1, a_p + n1, b_p + Tlen - n1)
    
    ## ============================
    ## 3. Sample mu and sigma^2 (all days, jumps removed)
    ## ============================
    prec_mu <- 1 / tau^2 + Tlen / sigma2
    mu      <- rnorm(1, mean = (sum(R - Z) / sigma2) / prec_mu, sd = sqrt(1 / prec_mu))
    sigma2  <- rinvgamma(1, shape = alpha0 + Tlen / 2,
                         rate = beta0 + 0.5 * sum((R - mu - Z)^2))
    
    ## ============================
    ## 4. Sample mu_J and sigma_J^2 (sampled jump sizes)
    ## ============================
    prec_J  <- 1 / tau^2 + n1 / sigmaJ2
    mu_J    <- rnorm(1, mean = (sum(Z[Y]) / sigmaJ2) / prec_J, sd = sqrt(1 / prec_J))
    sigmaJ2 <- rinvgamma(1, shape = alpha0 + n1 / 2,
                         rate = beta0 + 0.5 * sum((Z[Y] - mu_J)^2))
    
    ## ============================
    ## 5. Store JD parameters after burn-in + thinning
    ## ============================
    if (iter %in% keep_idx) {
      iter_keep <- iter_keep + 1L
      draws[iter_keep, ] <- c(mu, sqrt(sigma2), p, mu_J, sqrt(sigmaJ2))
    }
  }
  
  list(
    draws   = draws,
    R       = R,
    n_iter  = n_iter,
    burnin  = burnin,
    thin    = thin,
    hyper_p = hyper_p,
    hyper_mv = hyper_mv
  )
}

## ================================================
## Run Gibbs sampler for each regime
## ================================================

set.seed(789)  # reproducibility for Gibbs

regimes <- c("low", "medium", "high")
param_names <- c("mu", "sigma", "p", "mu_J", "sigma_J")

gibbs_list <- lapply(regimes, function(reg) {
  R_reg <- sim_jd[[reg]]$R
  gibbs_jd(R_reg,
           n_iter = 10000,
           burnin = 2000,
           thin   = 10)
})
names(gibbs_list) <- regimes

## Posterior summaries: mean, median, sd and 95% credible interval
## (the posterior of p is skewed when jumps are rare, so the median is reported too)
summary_gibbs <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(regimes, function(reg) {
    draws <- gibbs_list[[reg]]$draws

    post_mean   <- colMeans(draws)
    post_median <- apply(draws, 2, median)
    post_sd     <- apply(draws, 2, sd)
    post_lo     <- apply(draws, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025)
    post_hi     <- apply(draws, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975)

    true_par <- jd_params[[reg]]
    true_vec <- unlist(true_par)[param_names]

    data.frame(
      regime      = reg,
      parameter   = param_names,
      true_value  = true_vec,
      post_mean   = round(as.numeric(post_mean[param_names]), 4),
      post_median = round(as.numeric(post_median[param_names]), 4),
      post_sd     = round(as.numeric(post_sd[param_names]), 4),
      ci_2.5      = round(as.numeric(post_lo[param_names]), 4),
      ci_97.5     = round(as.numeric(post_hi[param_names]), 4),
      row.names   = NULL
    )
  })
)

summary_gibbs

## Quantities used in the text below
g_low_p      <- gibbs_list$low$draws[, "p"]
g_low_mean   <- mean(g_low_p)
g_low_median <- median(g_low_p)
```

The Gibbs sampler provides a fully Bayesian alternative to the MLE and EM
estimators and exhibits performance patterns consistent with the degree of jump
activity in each regime. In the medium- and high-risk settings, where the data
contain a sufficiently large number of jump observations, the posterior
distributions concentrate tightly around the true parameter values, and the
posterior means for \(\mu\), \(\sigma\), \(p\), \(\mu_J\), and \(\sigma_J\)
closely match both the simulation truth and the estimates obtained from the MLE
and EM algorithms. The posterior standard deviations in these regimes are small
and stable, reflecting well-identified mixture components and a likelihood that
provides strong information about both the diffusion and jump structures.

In contrast, the low-risk regime once again highlights the fundamental
identifiability issues that arise when jump events are extremely rare. The
posterior distributions for the jump probability \(p\) and the jump magnitude
parameters \(\mu_J\) and \(\sigma_J\) become diffuse, with large posterior
variances and noticeable shrinkage toward the diffusion component. The posterior
mean of \(p\) is `r round(g_low_mean, 4)`, about `r round(g_low_mean / jd_params$low$p, 1)` times its
true value: with only `r sum(Y_low)` jumps in the data, the \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,9)\) prior, whose
mean is 0.1, has a strong influence. Because the posterior of \(p\) is right-skewed,
its median (`r round(g_low_median, 4)`) is a better point summary than its mean, but it
is still well above the truth. This behavior
is not a computational artifact but a direct consequence of the limited
information in the data: when only a handful of observations could plausibly be
jumps, the posterior cannot sharply distinguish between the two mixture
components. Nevertheless, the Bayesian framework still yields coherent and
interpretable summaries of uncertainty, providing a transparent quantification
of precisely how weakly the data inform the jump component in this setting.

Overall, the Gibbs sampler performs comparably to the MLE and EM approaches in
well-identified regimes while offering the additional advantage of full
posterior uncertainty quantification. Its behavior in the low-jump regime also
reinforces a key theme observed throughout the analysis: accurate estimation of
jump characteristics fundamentally requires a sufficient number of jump events,
regardless of the estimation method employed.

### Sensitivity to the prior on the jump probability

Since the prior on \(p\) matters in the low regime, we rerun the Gibbs sampler on
the same low-regime data under two other priors: \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,49)\), whose
mean 0.02 is close to the true value, and the uniform \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\), which
expresses no preference for rare jumps. All other priors are unchanged.

```{r gibbs-prior-sensitivity}
## Low regime: Gibbs sampler under three priors for p
set.seed(2024)
prior_p_list <- list(
  "Beta(1, 9): mean 0.10"  = c(a = 1, b = 9),
  "Beta(1, 49): mean 0.02" = c(a = 1, b = 49),
  "Beta(1, 1): uniform"    = c(a = 1, b = 1)
)

## Under a flat prior the sampler occasionally wanders to large p (the "fake jump" region),
## so each prior gets 4 long chains, and their agreement is checked with the R-hat statistic.
split_rhat <- function(chains) {
  halves <- unlist(lapply(chains, function(x) { n <- floor(length(x) / 2)
    list(x[1:n], x[(n + 1):(2 * n)]) }), recursive = FALSE)
  n <- length(halves[[1]]); B <- n * var(sapply(halves, mean)); W <- mean(sapply(halves, var))
  sqrt(((n - 1) / n * W + B / n) / W)
}
sens_chains <- lapply(prior_p_list, function(hp) {
  lapply(1:4, function(k) gibbs_jd(R_low, n_iter = 40000, burnin = 5000, thin = 10, hyper_p = hp)$draws)
})
sens_draws <- lapply(sens_chains, function(ch) do.call(rbind, ch))

prior_sens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sens_draws), function(nm) {
  d <- sens_draws[[nm]]
  data.frame(
    `Prior for p`      = nm,
    `p median`         = median(d[, "p"]),
    `p mean`           = mean(d[, "p"]),
    `p 2.5%`           = unname(quantile(d[, "p"], 0.025)),
    `p 97.5%`          = unname(quantile(d[, "p"], 0.975)),
    `mu_J median`      = median(d[, "mu_J"]),
    `sigma_J median`   = median(d[, "sigma_J"]),
    `R-hat (p)`        = split_rhat(lapply(sens_chains[[nm]], function(x) x[, "p"])),
    check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
  )
}))

knitr::kable(prior_sens, digits = 4, booktabs = TRUE,
             caption = paste0("Low regime (true p = 0.01, mu_J = -0.015, sigma_J = 0.01; ",
                              sum(Y_low), " jumps in the data): posterior of the jump ",
                              "parameters under three priors for p."))

sens_p_median <- setNames(prior_sens$`p median`, c("b9", "b49", "unif"))
```

Each row pools four chains of 35,000 iterations after burn-in, and the R-hat
values close to 1 show that the chains agree. The prior matters, but less than
the width of the posterior. The posterior median of \(p\) is
`r round(sens_p_median["b49"], 4)` under \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,49)\),
`r round(sens_p_median["b9"], 4)` under \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,9)\) and
`r round(sens_p_median["unif"], 4)` under the uniform prior, and the upper end of the
95\% credible interval rises from `r round(prior_sens[2, "p 97.5%"], 3)` to
`r round(prior_sens[1, "p 97.5%"], 3)` to `r round(prior_sens[3, "p 97.5%"], 3)`. Even
with no preference for rare jumps, these data favour a jump probability of a few
percent, above the true 1\%: with about `r sum(Y_low)` jumps among `r n_obs` days,
the likelihood cannot distinguish a few large jumps from more frequent small ones.
Under the uniform prior the sampler also makes occasional excursions to much larger
values of \(p\), where the "jump" component describes ordinary days; short runs can
miss or overweight these excursions, which is why long, multiple chains are needed
here. In this regime the data identify the diffusion part of the model well but say
little about the jump frequency, and a Bayesian estimate of \(p\) should be reported
together with the prior it depends on.

## Bayesian estimation with Stan

The jump-diffusion specification
\[
R_t = \mu + \sigma \varepsilon_t + Y_t Z_t,\qquad t = 1,\dots,T,
\]
with
\[
\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1), \quad
Y_t \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p), \quad
Z_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_J,\sigma_J^2),
\]
implies that the marginal distribution of each return is a two-component
Gaussian mixture,
\[
R_t \mid \theta \sim (1-p)\,\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)
\;+\;
p\,\mathcal{N}\bigl(\mu + \mu_J,\;\sigma^2 + \sigma_J^2\bigr),
\]
where
\[
\theta = (\mu,\sigma,p,\mu_J,\sigma_J)
\]
denotes the vector of unknown model parameters. The corresponding
observed-data likelihood for a sample $R_1,\dots,R_T$ is
\[
L(\theta;R_{1:T})
=
\prod_{t=1}^T
\left[
(1-p)\,\phi(R_t;\mu,\sigma^2)
+
p\,\phi\bigl(R_t;\mu+\mu_J,\sigma^2+\sigma_J^2\bigr)
\right],
\]
with $\phi(\cdot;m,v)$ the normal density with mean $m$ and variance $v$.
Rather than introducing latent indicators $Y_t$ explicitly, the Stan
implementation works directly with this marginalized mixture likelihood.

\paragraph{Bayesian formulation.}
In the Bayesian framework, the unknown parameters $\theta$ are treated
as random and assigned prior distributions. We use exactly the same
priors as in the Gibbs sampler,
\[
p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(1,9),\qquad
\mu,\ \mu_J \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\,0.05^2),
\]
\[
\sigma^2 \sim \mathrm{Inv{\text-}Gamma}(2,\,2\times10^{-4}),\qquad
\sigma_J^2 \sim \mathrm{Inv{\text-}Gamma}(2,\,2\times10^{-4}),
\]
so the Stan model is parameterized by the variances $\sigma^2$ and
$\sigma_J^2$, and $\sigma$ and $\sigma_J$ are reported as their square
roots. The two Bayesian methods therefore target the same posterior
distribution and differ only in the sampling algorithm. This makes the
comparison informative: any difference between Gibbs and Stan beyond
Monte Carlo error would point to an error in one of the two
implementations.

Given these priors, the posterior density is
\[
\pi(\theta \mid R_{1:T})
\;\propto\;
L(\theta;R_{1:T})\,
\pi(\mu)\,\pi(\sigma^2)\,\pi(p)\,\pi(\mu_J)\,\pi(\sigma_J^2),
\]
and forms the basis for Bayesian inference on both point estimates and
uncertainty.

\paragraph{Stan implementation and sampling.}
In the Stan code, the mixture likelihood contribution of each
observation is evaluated using the numerically stable \texttt{log\_mix}
function. For each $t$,
\[
\log f(R_t \mid \theta)
=
\log\Bigl[
(1-p)\,\phi(R_t;\mu,\sigma^2)
+
p\,\phi\bigl(R_t;\mu+\mu_J,\sigma^2+\sigma_J^2\bigr)
\Bigr]
\]
is computed internally as
\[
\texttt{target += log\_mix}\bigl(
p,\,
\log \phi(R_t;\mu+\mu_J,\sigma^2+\sigma_J^2),\,
\log \phi(R_t;\mu,\sigma^2)
\bigr),
\]
which avoids numerical underflow when one component has very small
weight or extremely low density for a given $R_t$. Summing these terms
over $t=1,\dots,T$ yields the log-likelihood, to which the (log-)priors
for $\theta$ are added in the \texttt{model} block.

Stan then uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with the No-U-Turn Sampler
(NUTS) to draw approximate samples from the joint posterior
$\pi(\theta \mid R_{1:T})$. The sampler operates on the continuous
parameter vector $\theta$ only; no discrete latent indicators $Y_t$ are
introduced, which is crucial because Stan does not support discrete
parameters. After discarding warmup iterations used for adaptation, the
remaining draws
\[
\{\theta^{(s)}\}_{s=1}^S
\]
provide Monte Carlo approximations to posterior expectations and
uncertainty measures. In particular, posterior means and standard
deviations for each component of $\theta$ are reported as Bayesian
analogues of point estimates and standard errors, together with
convergence diagnostics such as the potential scale reduction factor
$\widehat{R}$ and effective sample sizes.

```{r stan-jd-setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Stan implementation for the jump–diffusion mixture model
# Requires: R_low, R_medium, R_high already defined

# If needed:
# install.packages("rstan")
library(rstan)
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

stan_code_jd <- "
data {
  int<lower=1> T;           // number of observations
  vector[T] R;              // returns
}
parameters {
  real mu;                  // drift
  real<lower=0> sigma2;     // diffusion variance
  real<lower=0, upper=1> p; // jump probability
  real mu_J;                // jump mean
  real<lower=0> sigma_J2;   // jump variance
}
model {
  real sigma   = sqrt(sigma2);
  real sd_jump = sqrt(sigma2 + sigma_J2);

  // -- Priors: identical to the Gibbs sampler --
  mu       ~ normal(0, 0.05);
  mu_J     ~ normal(0, 0.05);
  sigma2   ~ inv_gamma(2, 2e-4);
  sigma_J2 ~ inv_gamma(2, 2e-4);
  p        ~ beta(1, 9);          // prior mean 0.10, favors rare jumps

  // -- Likelihood: 2-component Gaussian mixture --
  for (t in 1:T) {
    // Mixture: p * jump + (1 - p) * no-jump
    target += log_mix(p,
                      normal_lpdf(R[t] | mu + mu_J, sd_jump),
                      normal_lpdf(R[t] | mu, sigma));
  }
}
generated quantities {
  // Standard deviations, for reporting on the same scale as the other methods
  real sigma   = sqrt(sigma2);
  real sigma_J = sqrt(sigma_J2);
}
"

# Compile the Stan model (reused in the real-data section)
jd_stan_model <- stan_model(model_code = stan_code_jd)

# Helper to build Stan data list from a return series
make_stan_data <- function(R) {
  list(
    T = length(R),
    R = as.vector(R)
  )
}

# Fit for each regime (you can comment out some of these while testing)
fit_stan_low <- sampling(
  jd_stan_model,
  data   = make_stan_data(R_low),
  chains = 4,
  iter   = 4000,
  warmup = 2000,
  seed   = 2025
)

fit_stan_medium <- sampling(
  jd_stan_model,
  data   = make_stan_data(R_medium),
  chains = 4,
  iter   = 4000,
  warmup = 2000,
  seed   = 2025
)

fit_stan_high <- sampling(
  jd_stan_model,
  data   = make_stan_data(R_high),
  chains = 4,
  iter   = 4000,
  warmup = 2000,
  seed   = 2025
)

# Posterior summaries and convergence diagnostics
pars_jd   <- c("mu", "sigma", "p", "mu_J", "sigma_J")
stan_fits <- list(low = fit_stan_low, medium = fit_stan_medium, high = fit_stan_high)

summary_stan <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(stan_fits), function(reg) {
  s <- rstan::summary(stan_fits[[reg]], pars = pars_jd,
                      probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))$summary
  data.frame(
    regime      = reg,
    parameter   = pars_jd,
    true_value  = unlist(jd_params[[reg]])[pars_jd],
    post_mean   = s[, "mean"],
    post_median = s[, "50%"],
    post_sd     = s[, "sd"],
    ci_2.5      = s[, "2.5%"],
    ci_97.5     = s[, "97.5%"],
    n_eff       = round(s[, "n_eff"]),
    Rhat        = s[, "Rhat"],
    row.names   = NULL
  )
}))
knitr::kable(summary_stan, digits = 4, booktabs = TRUE,
             caption = "Stan posterior summaries (4 chains) with effective sample sizes and R-hat.")

# Divergent transitions after warmup (should be 0)
stan_divergences <- sapply(stan_fits, rstan::get_num_divergent)
stan_divergences
stan_max_rhat <- max(summary_stan$Rhat)
```

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The Bayesian estimation results obtained through Stan demonstrate that the
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo approach provides a stable and effective framework for
inferring the parameters of the jump-diffusion model across all simulation
regimes. In the medium- and high-risk settings, the posterior distributions for
$\mu$, $\sigma$, $p$, $\mu_J$, and $\sigma_J$ are sharply concentrated around the
true values, confirming that Stan successfully recovers both the continuous and
jump components of the model when the data contain sufficient jump information.
In the low-risk regime, where jump events are rare and the mixture components
overlap substantially, the posterior correctly reflects the corresponding
identifiability limitations: the drift remains well estimated, and the posterior for the diffusion volatility is tight, while jump-related parameters exhibit wider posterior uncertainty. Importantly, unlike the MLE—which may suffer from singular Hessians
or boundary estimates—Bayesian inference via NUTS remains numerically robust and
provides full posterior uncertainty quantification without relying on resampling
methods. Overall, the Stan implementation offers a principled and reliable
Bayesian alternative to MLE and EM, performing comparably in well-identified
settings while delivering more informative uncertainty assessments in difficult
low-jump environments. The sampler reported `r sum(stan_divergences)` divergent
transitions across the three regimes, and the largest \(\widehat{R}\) is
`r round(stan_max_rhat, 3)`, so there is no sign of convergence problems.

```{r comparison-table, echo=FALSE}
## Comparison table computed from the fits above
## (posterior medians for Gibbs and Stan, since the posterior of p is skewed)
stan_median <- function(fit) {
  rstan::summary(fit, pars = param_names, probs = 0.5)$summary[param_names, "50%"]
}
comparison_sim <- do.call(rbind, lapply(regimes, function(reg) {
  data.frame(
    Regime         = reg,
    Parameter      = param_names,
    True           = unlist(jd_params[[reg]])[param_names],
    MLE            = fit_list[[reg]]$par_theta[param_names],
    EM             = fit_em_list[[reg]]$par_theta[param_names],
    `Gibbs Median` = apply(gibbs_list[[reg]]$draws, 2, median)[param_names],
    `Stan Median`  = stan_median(stan_fits[[reg]]),
    check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}))
knitr::kable(comparison_sim, digits = 4, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Comparison of Jump-Diffusion Parameter Estimates Across Four Estimation Methods (Gibbs and Stan: posterior medians).")

## Quantities used in the text below
low_p_ratio <- with(subset(comparison_sim, Regime == "low" & Parameter == "p"),
                    c(gibbs = `Gibbs Median` / True, stan = `Stan Median` / True))
```

\paragraph{Comparison of Estimation Methods.}
Across the three simulation regimes, the four estimation approaches—MLE,
EM, Gibbs sampling, and Stan—exhibit distinct behaviors that reflect their
underlying inferential philosophies and numerical properties. In the
medium- and high-risk regimes, where jump events are frequent enough to
provide clear separation between mixture components, all methods recover
the true parameters with high accuracy. The diffusion parameters $(\mu,
\sigma)$ are estimated almost identically across MLE, EM, Gibbs, and Stan,
and the jump parameters $(p, \mu_J, \sigma_J)$ are also well identified,
with only modest differences attributable to sampling variability and
prior smoothing in the Bayesian methods. The two Bayesian methods use
the same priors and target the same posterior, so their posterior
medians should agree up to Monte Carlo error, and they do.

The low-risk regime illustrates the core challenge: when jump events are
rare, the mixture likelihood becomes weakly identified. MLE and EM, which
maximize the same likelihood, give the same estimates: on this dataset the
jump probability is close to its true value, but the jump-size standard
deviation collapses toward zero and the bootstrap standard error of $p$ is
more than twenty-five times the estimate, consistent with the well-known
pathology of finite-mixture likelihoods with tiny component weights. The
Bayesian methods (Gibbs and Stan) avoid the collapse of $\sigma_J$, but their
posterior medians of $p$ are `r round(low_p_ratio["gibbs"], 1)` and
`r round(low_p_ratio["stan"], 1)` times the truth, because the prior has
a strong influence when only a handful of jumps are observed (see the
prior-sensitivity analysis above); their posterior
standard deviations correctly inflate to reflect the lack of information. In
this regime no method recovers the jump parameters reliably: the limiting
factor is the information in the data, not the estimation method.

Overall, the comparison reveals that: (i) in well-identified regimes, all
methods perform similarly; (ii) in weak-signal regimes, no method recovers
the jump parameters reliably: MLE and EM agree but can place $\sigma_J$ on the
boundary, the Bayesian estimates of $p$ are pulled toward the prior, and the
Bayesian approaches (Gibbs, Stan) give the most honest picture of the
uncertainty; and (iii) careful implementation matters as much as the choice
of method: with a correctly specified EM algorithm and Gibbs sampler and a
robust optimizer for the MLE, all four methods agree whenever the data
contain enough jumps.

## Monte Carlo study: performance over repeated samples

The comparison above uses one simulated dataset per regime, and a single
dataset can be lucky or unlucky. To see how the estimators behave on
average, we simulate 100 new datasets per regime from the same model
and apply the MLE, the EM algorithm and the Gibbs sampler to each (Stan is
left out to keep the computing time reasonable; it targets the same
posterior as the Gibbs sampler). The Gibbs point estimate is the posterior
median. For each regime and method we report the median of
\(\hat p / p\) (1 means unbiased in the median), the median absolute error
of \(\hat p\) relative to \(p\), the medians of \(\hat\mu_J/\mu_J\) and
\(\hat\sigma_J/\sigma_J\), the share of datasets in which the estimate of
\(\sigma_J\) collapsed (below 10\% of its true value), and, for the Gibbs
sampler, the share of datasets in which the 95\% credible interval for
\(p\) contains the true value.

```{r monte-carlo, cache=TRUE}
## Monte Carlo study: n_mc datasets per regime; MLE, EM and Gibbs on each.
## Each dataset has its own seed, so results do not depend on the number of cores.
## (cache = TRUE: re-knitting does not recompute this chunk unless its code changes)
n_mc <- 100

mc_one <- function(reg, r) {
  set.seed(100000 * match(reg, c("low", "medium", "high")) + r)
  par <- jd_params[[reg]]
  R <- simulate_jump_diffusion(n_obs, par$mu, par$sigma, par$p, par$mu_J, par$sigma_J)$R

  mle <- fit_jd_mle_simple(R)
  em  <- fit_em_jd(R)
  d   <- gibbs_jd(R, n_iter = 4000, burnin = 1000, thin = 3)$draws
  ci  <- quantile(d[, "p"], c(0.025, 0.975))

  est <- rbind(MLE   = mle$par_theta[param_names],
               EM    = em$par_theta[param_names],
               Gibbs = apply(d, 2, median)[param_names])
  data.frame(regime = reg, rep = r, method = rownames(est), est,
             logLik  = c(mle$logLik, em$logLik, NA),
             covered = c(NA, NA, ci[1] <= par$p && par$p <= ci[2]),
             row.names = NULL)
}

jobs <- expand.grid(r = seq_len(n_mc), reg = c("low", "medium", "high"),
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

## Run in parallel (works on Windows, macOS and Linux)
n_cores <- max(1L, parallel::detectCores() - 1L)
cl <- parallel::makeCluster(n_cores)
fun_names <- Filter(function(nm) is.function(get(nm)), ls())
parallel::clusterExport(cl, c(fun_names, "jobs", "jd_params", "n_obs", "param_names"),
                        envir = environment())
mc_raw <- do.call(rbind, parallel::parLapply(cl, seq_len(nrow(jobs)),
                                             function(i) mc_one(jobs$reg[i], jobs$r[i])))
parallel::stopCluster(cl)
```

```{r monte-carlo-summary}
options(knitr.kable.NA = "-")
mc_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("low", "medium", "high"), function(reg) {
  tp <- jd_params[[reg]]
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("MLE", "EM", "Gibbs"), function(m) {
    d <- mc_raw[mc_raw$regime == reg & mc_raw$method == m, ]
    data.frame(
      Regime                  = reg,
      Method                  = m,
      `median p-hat/p`        = median(d$p / tp$p),
      `median abs. error / p` = median(abs(d$p - tp$p)) / tp$p,
      `median mu_J-hat/mu_J`  = median(d$mu_J / tp$mu_J),
      `median sigma_J-hat/sigma_J` = median(d$sigma_J / tp$sigma_J),
      `sigma_J collapsed`     = mean(d$sigma_J < 0.1 * tp$sigma_J),
      `95% coverage of p`     = if (m == "Gibbs") mean(d$covered) else NA,
      check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
    )
  }))
}))
knitr::kable(mc_summary, digits = 2, booktabs = TRUE,
             caption = paste0("Monte Carlo study: ", n_mc,
                              " simulated datasets per regime (T = ", n_obs, ")."))

## Quantities used in the text below
mc_val <- function(reg, m, col) mc_summary[mc_summary$Regime == reg & mc_summary$Method == m, col]
ll_wide  <- reshape(mc_raw[mc_raw$method != "Gibbs", c("regime", "rep", "method", "logLik")],
                    idvar = c("regime", "rep"), timevar = "method", direction = "wide")
em_gap   <- ll_wide$logLik.MLE - ll_wide$logLik.EM
share_em_matches <- mean(abs(em_gap) < 0.01)
```

The MLE and EM reach the same maximum of the likelihood (within 0.01 in
log-likelihood) in `r round(100 * share_em_matches)`\% of all datasets, which
confirms that the corrected EM algorithm maximizes the jump-diffusion likelihood.
In the medium and high regimes all three estimators are close to the truth in
the median, with \(\hat p / p\) between
`r round(min(mc_summary[mc_summary$Regime != "low", "median p-hat/p"]), 2)` and
`r round(max(mc_summary[mc_summary$Regime != "low", "median p-hat/p"]), 2)`.
The Gibbs 95\% credible intervals contain the true \(p\) in
`r round(100 * mc_val("medium", "Gibbs", "95% coverage of p"))`\% of the
medium-regime datasets, close to the nominal 95\%, but only in
`r round(100 * mc_val("high", "Gibbs", "95% coverage of p"))`\% of the
high-regime datasets. The likely cause is the prior on the jump variance: the
\(\mathrm{Inv{\text-}Gamma}(2,\,2\times10^{-4})\) prior favours small values of
\(\sigma_J^2\), and the Gibbs estimates of \(\sigma_J\) are
`r round(mc_val("medium", "Gibbs", "median sigma_J-hat/sigma_J"), 2)` and
`r round(mc_val("high", "Gibbs", "median sigma_J-hat/sigma_J"), 2)` times the
truth in the medium and high regimes, against
`r round(mc_val("medium", "MLE", "median sigma_J-hat/sigma_J"), 2)` and
`r round(mc_val("high", "MLE", "median sigma_J-hat/sigma_J"), 2)` for the MLE.
A smaller \(\sigma_J\) makes jumps harder to tell apart from ordinary days, so
fewer days are attributed to jumps and \(p\) is underestimated as well.

The low regime behaves differently, and the repeated samples show that the
single-dataset results above were typical rather than unlucky. The MLE and EM
underestimate \(p\) (median ratio
`r round(mc_val("low", "MLE", "median p-hat/p"), 2)`), their median absolute
error is `r round(100 * mc_val("low", "MLE", "median abs. error / p"))`\% of the
true value, and the estimate of \(\sigma_J\) collapses toward zero in
`r round(100 * mc_val("low", "MLE", "sigma_J collapsed"))`\% of the datasets.
The Gibbs sampler never collapses, because the same inverse-gamma prior keeps
\(\sigma_J^2\) away from zero, but its estimate of \(p\) is pulled upward toward
the prior (median ratio `r round(mc_val("low", "Gibbs", "median p-hat/p"), 2)`),
while its credible intervals contain the true value in
`r round(100 * mc_val("low", "Gibbs", "95% coverage of p"))`\% of the datasets.

The prior on the jump variance is therefore a trade-off: it stabilizes
estimation when jumps are rare and introduces a modest downward bias when they
are frequent. More generally, with around 20 jumps in 2000 days the frequentist
estimates are noisy and the Bayesian ones depend on the prior; the uncertainty
is a property of the data, and the most useful thing an estimator can do is to
report it honestly.

\section{Real-World Application of the Jump-Diffusion Estimation Methods}

Having established the behavior of MLE, EM, Gibbs sampling, and Stan through a controlled simulation study, we now turn to real financial return data to examine whether the same patterns hold in practice. We select three assets representing low-, medium-, and high-risk regimes:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{JNJ (low risk)} - stable, defensive equity,
  \item \textbf{SPY (medium risk)} - broad market index,
  \item \textbf{TSLA (high risk)} - highly volatile growth stock.
\end{itemize}
Daily log-returns from 2015-2024 are used to ensure a long sample with sufficient jump events for reliable estimation.

All four estimation methods were applied using the same procedures validated in the simulation study. The resulting parameter estimates are summarized in the comparison table.

```{r check-internet, include=FALSE}
## The real-data section needs to download prices from Yahoo Finance.
has_internet <- !inherits(try(quantmod::getSymbols("SPY", from = "2024-12-02", to = "2024-12-06",
                                                    auto.assign = FALSE), silent = TRUE), "try-error")
```

```{r real-data, eval=has_internet}
library(rstan)
library(quantmod)
library(dplyr)

## ----------------------
## 1. Setup: tickers and date range
## ----------------------
tickers <- c(low = "JNJ",
             medium = "SPY",
             high = "TSLA")

start_date <- "2015-01-01"
end_date   <- "2024-12-31"

## ----------------------
## 2. Download and merge adjusted prices
## ----------------------
get_prices <- function(sym) {
  Ad(getSymbols(sym, from = start_date, to = end_date, auto.assign = FALSE))
}

px_list <- lapply(tickers, get_prices)

# Merge on dates; this creates an xts with all columns
all_px <- do.call(merge, px_list)

# Give nice column names (low, medium, high)
colnames(all_px) <- names(tickers)

# Keep only dates where ALL three tickers have data
all_px_cc <- na.omit(all_px)

## ----------------------
## 3. Compute log-returns on the common period
## ----------------------
all_ret <- diff(log(all_px_cc))

# Drop the first row created by diff (it will be NA)
all_ret <- all_ret[complete.cases(all_ret), ]

# Build a list of numeric return vectors for each regime
returns_list <- list(
  low    = as.numeric(all_ret[, "low"]),
  medium = as.numeric(all_ret[, "medium"]),
  high   = as.numeric(all_ret[, "high"])
)

## ----------------------
## 4. Quick plots: prices and returns
## ----------------------
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(3, 4, 3, 1))

# Price paths
plot(all_px_cc[, "low"],    main = paste0("Price: ", tickers["low"]),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Price", col = "black")
plot(all_px_cc[, "medium"], main = paste0("Price: ", tickers["medium"]),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Price", col = "black")
plot(all_px_cc[, "high"],   main = paste0("Price: ", tickers["high"]),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Price", col = "black")

# Return series
plot(all_ret[, "low"],    main = paste0("Returns: ", tickers["low"]),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Log-return", col = "black")
plot(all_ret[, "medium"], main = paste0("Returns: ", tickers["medium"]),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Log-return", col = "black")
plot(all_ret[, "high"],   main = paste0("Returns: ", tickers["high"]),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Log-return", col = "black")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

## ----------------------
## 5. Summary table (no NA problems)
## ----------------------
summary_df <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(names(returns_list), function(reg) {
    r <- returns_list[[reg]]
    r <- r[is.finite(r)]  # extra safety, should already be fine

    data.frame(
      regime   = reg,
      ticker   = tickers[reg],
      n        = length(r),
      mean     = mean(r, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd       = sd(r, na.rm = TRUE),
      min      = min(r, na.rm = TRUE),
      q25      = quantile(r, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
      median   = median(r, na.rm = TRUE),
      q75      = quantile(r, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
      max      = max(r, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
  })
)

summary_df



# Plot log-price and returns for each ticker
par(mfrow = c(3, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (reg in names(tickers)) {
  symbol <- tickers[reg]
  x <- getSymbols(symbol, from = start_date, to = end_date, auto.assign = FALSE)
  px <- Ad(x)
  ts.plot(log(px), main = paste0(symbol, " (", reg, ") - log price"),
          ylab = "log(price)", xlab = "Time")
  
  r <- returns_list[[reg]]
  ts.plot(r, main = paste0(symbol, " (", reg, ") - log returns"),
          ylab = "return", xlab = "Time")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

## ================================================
## 2.-4. MLE, EM and Gibbs sampler
## ================================================
## The real-data fits use the same (corrected) functions defined in the
## simulation study above: fit_jd_mle_simple(), fit_em_jd() and gibbs_jd().
param_names <- c("mu", "sigma", "p", "mu_J", "sigma_J")

## ================================================
## 5. Stan model: the model compiled in the simulation study (jd_stan_model)
##    is reused here, with the same priors as the Gibbs sampler.
## ================================================

## ================================================
## 6. Fit all four methods on each regime
## ================================================
regimes <- names(tickers)

fit_results <- lapply(regimes, function(reg) {
  R_reg <- returns_list[[reg]]
  
  # MLE
  fit_mle <- fit_jd_mle_simple(R_reg)
  
  # EM
  fit_em  <- fit_em_jd(R_reg)
  
  # Gibbs
  gibbs_fit <- gibbs_jd(R_reg, n_iter = 6000, burnin = 2000, thin = 5)
  gibbs_draws <- gibbs_fit$draws
  gibbs_median <- apply(gibbs_draws, 2, median)
  
  # Stan
  fit_stan <- sampling(
    jd_stan_model,
    data   = make_stan_data(R_reg),
    chains = 4,
    iter   = 3000,
    warmup = 1500,
    seed   = 2025,
    refresh = 0
  )
  stan_sum <- summary(fit_stan, pars = param_names, probs = 0.5)$summary
  stan_median <- stan_sum[, "50%"]
  names(stan_median) <- rownames(stan_sum)
  
  list(
    mle   = fit_mle$par_theta,
    em    = fit_em$par_theta,
    gibbs = gibbs_median[param_names],
    stan  = stan_median[param_names],
    stan_divergences = rstan::get_num_divergent(fit_stan)
  )
})
names(fit_results) <- regimes

## ================================================
## 7. Final comparison table
## ================================================
comparison_table <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(regimes, function(reg) {
    mats <- fit_results[[reg]]
    data.frame(
      regime   = reg,
      ticker   = tickers[reg],
      parameter = param_names,
      MLE      = round(as.numeric(mats$mle[param_names]),   5),
      EM       = round(as.numeric(mats$em[param_names]),    5),
      Gibbs    = round(as.numeric(mats$gibbs[param_names]), 5),
      Stan     = round(as.numeric(mats$stan[param_names]),  5),
      row.names = NULL
    )
  })
)

print(comparison_table)   # Gibbs and Stan: posterior medians

# Divergent transitions in the Stan fits (should be 0)
sapply(fit_results, function(x) x$stan_divergences)
```

\subsection*{Conclusions from Real-World Estimation}

Across all three assets, we observe a high degree of agreement between the four estimation methods. Unlike the simulated low-risk regime, where extremely rare jumps made the jump parameters hard to estimate, the real data produce much larger estimated jump probabilities, and all estimators find the same solution. Several key conclusions emerge:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Low-risk asset (JNJ).} 
  The diffusion volatility is small (\(\sigma \approx 0.008\)), the estimated jump probability is about 10\%, and estimated jump sizes are small and negative. All methods agree closely.

  \item \textbf{Medium-risk asset (SPY).}
  Volatility is at a typical market level (\(\sigma \approx 0.007\)), with jump probabilities around 16\%. The jump mean is slightly negative, in line with downside market shocks.

  \item \textbf{High-risk asset (TSLA).}
  Volatility is extremely high (\(\sigma \approx 0.022\)), and the estimated jump probability is very large (\(p \approx 0.25\)). Jumps are roughly symmetric (\(\mu_J \approx 0\)), consistent with both large upward and downward moves.
\end{enumerate}

Across all assets, MLE, EM, Gibbs, and Stan deliver nearly identical point estimates, so the four methods compute the same thing reliably on real data. Agreement between methods does not, however, show that the model describes the data well; that question is taken up next.

A caution on interpretation. Estimated jump probabilities of this size, with average jumps comparable to ordinary daily moves, do not describe rare jumps. Because the model treats days as independent, its jump component also absorbs fat tails and volatility clustering (alternating calm and turbulent periods), which are pronounced in daily stock returns.

\paragraph{A test of independent jumps.}
The model can be checked directly. At the EM estimates we compute, for every day, the probability that it contains a jump given its return, \(P(Y_t = 1 \mid R_t)\), and flag the days on which this probability exceeds one half. If jumps occur independently with a constant probability, as the model assumes, the flagged days should be spread evenly over time. We divide the sample into years (blocks of 250 days for the simulated data) and apply a chi-square test of an even spread, with the expected counts proportional to the number of days in each year and the p-value computed by simulation. We first apply the test to the simulated data, where jumps are independent by construction, to confirm that it works when the model is true: once to the single dataset of each regime, and once to each of the 100 Monte Carlo datasets per regime, to check that it rejects in about 5\% of cases.

```{r flag-test-simulated}
## Posterior probability that day t contains a jump, P(Y_t = 1 | R_t), given parameters theta
jump_prob <- function(theta, R) {
  log_f0 <- log1p(-theta["p"]) + dnorm(R, theta["mu"], theta["sigma"], log = TRUE)
  log_f1 <- log(theta["p"]) + dnorm(R, theta["mu"] + theta["mu_J"],
                                    sqrt(theta["sigma"]^2 + theta["sigma_J"]^2), log = TRUE)
  1 / (1 + exp(log_f0 - log_f1))
}

## Chi-square test that flagged days are spread evenly across blocks (years)
flag_test <- function(flags, block) {
  flags[is.na(flags)] <- FALSE
  counts <- tapply(flags, block, sum)
  n_days <- tapply(flags, block, length)
  if (sum(counts) < 2) return(c(flagged = sum(counts), p_value = NA))
  test <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(counts, p = n_days / sum(n_days),
                                      simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 4999))
  c(flagged = sum(counts), p_value = test$p.value)
}

sim_regimes <- c("low", "medium", "high")
sim_block   <- rep(seq_len(n_obs / 250), each = 250)   # 8 "years" of 250 days

## (a) The single simulated dataset of each regime, at its EM estimates
set.seed(321)
sim_flag_test <- t(sapply(sim_regimes, function(reg) {
  flag_test(jump_prob(fit_em_list[[reg]]$par_theta, sim_jd[[reg]]$R) > 0.5, sim_block)
}))
```
