```{r flag-test-simulated}
## (b) The Monte Carlo datasets: regenerate each with its seed, use its EM estimates
mc_em <- mc_raw[mc_raw$method == "EM", ]
mc_flag_p <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(mc_em)), function(i) {
  reg <- mc_em$regime[i]
  r   <- mc_em$rep[i]
  set.seed(100000 * match(reg, sim_regimes) + r)       # same seed as in the Monte Carlo study
  par <- jd_params[[reg]]
  R <- simulate_jump_diffusion(n_obs, par$mu, par$sigma, par$p, par$mu_J, par$sigma_J)$R
  theta <- unlist(mc_em[i, param_names])
  flag_test(jump_prob(theta, R) > 0.5, sim_block)["p_value"]
})
mc_reject <- tapply(mc_flag_p < 0.05, mc_em$regime, mean, na.rm = TRUE)[sim_regimes]

sim_flag_table <- data.frame(
  Data                    = paste("Simulated,", sim_regimes, "regime"),
  `Flagged days`          = sim_flag_test[, "flagged"],
  `p-value`               = format.pval(sim_flag_test[, "p_value"], digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
  `Rejection rate at 5% over 100 datasets` = round(as.numeric(mc_reject), 2),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
knitr::kable(sim_flag_table, booktabs = TRUE,
             caption = "Test of an even spread of flagged jump days: simulated data (independent jumps).")
```

```{r real-jump-prob, eval=has_internet, fig.height=7}
## The same test on the real data, with calendar years as blocks
ret_dates <- zoo::index(all_ret)
jump_prob_list <- lapply(regimes, function(reg) jump_prob(fit_results[[reg]]$em, returns_list[[reg]]))
names(jump_prob_list) <- regimes

par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(3, 4, 2, 1))
for (reg in regimes) {
  plot(ret_dates, jump_prob_list[[reg]], type = "h", ylim = c(0, 1),
       main = paste0(tickers[reg], ": probability that each day contains a jump"),
       xlab = "", ylab = "P(jump | return)")
  abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

## Number of flagged days (probability > 0.5) per year
years <- format(ret_dates, "%Y")
flag_year <- do.call(cbind, lapply(regimes, function(reg) tapply(jump_prob_list[[reg]] > 0.5, years, sum)))
colnames(flag_year) <- tickers[regimes]
knitr::kable(flag_year, booktabs = TRUE,
             caption = "Number of days per year with jump probability above 0.5.")

set.seed(654)
real_flag_test <- t(sapply(regimes, function(reg) flag_test(jump_prob_list[[reg]] > 0.5, years)))
real_flag_table <- data.frame(
  Data           = paste0("Real, ", tickers[regimes]),
  `Flagged days` = real_flag_test[, "flagged"],
  `p-value`      = format.pval(real_flag_test[, "p_value"], digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
knitr::kable(real_flag_table, booktabs = TRUE,
             caption = "Test of an even spread of flagged jump days: real data, 2015-2024.")
```

On the simulated data the test behaves as it should. Across the 100 Monte Carlo datasets it rejects an even spread at the 5\% level in `r round(100 * mc_reject["low"])`\%, `r round(100 * mc_reject["medium"])`\% and `r round(100 * mc_reject["high"])`\% of cases in the low, medium and high regimes, close to the nominal 5\%. On the real data it rejects for all three stocks, with simulated p-values `r if (has_internet) { if (all(real_flag_test[, "p_value"] < 0.001)) "below 0.001 in every case" else paste0("of ", paste(real_flag_table[["p-value"]], collapse = ", "), " for JNJ, SPY and TSLA") }`. The flagged days are concentrated in turbulent periods: SPY has `r if (has_internet) flag_year["2020", "SPY"]` flagged days in 2020 and `r if (has_internet) flag_year["2022", "SPY"]` in 2022, but only `r if (has_internet) flag_year["2017", "SPY"]` in 2017.

\paragraph{Limitation.}
The model assumes that days are independent and that the jump probability and the volatility are constant over time. In the simulation this holds by construction, so there the estimators behave as theory predicts: they recover the parameters when the data contain enough jumps, and their difficulties in the low regime come from the scarcity of jumps alone. In daily stock returns it does not hold: volatility moves through persistent calm and turbulent periods, and the test above detects this clearly. On real data the jump component therefore mixes genuine jumps with fat tails and volatility clustering, and its parameters should not be read as the frequency and size of jumps. Measuring jumps in real returns requires a model with time-varying volatility (for example GARCH or stochastic volatility), so that a move is judged relative to the volatility of its period; this is the natural next step for this work.

\section{Interpretation for Risk Management and Portfolio Decisions}

Subject to the limitation above, which matters most for the jump probability, the estimated jump-diffusion parameters have direct practical value for asset managers, risk teams, and quantitative portfolio strategists. Each parameter can be interpreted as follows:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Drift \(\mu\): expected daily return.}  
  This parameter helps calibrate expected long-term performance and risk premia. For daily data, \(\mu\) is typically small, as seen in the estimates.

  \item \textbf{Diffusion volatility \(\sigma\): ordinary day-to-day variability.}  
  This is the core input to standard risk metrics such as Value-at-Risk, volatility targeting, and mean–variance portfolio optimization. Assets with larger \(\sigma\) (e.g., TSLA) naturally call for smaller position sizes in risk-managed portfolios.

  \item \textbf{Jump probability \(p\): likelihood of sudden discontinuities.}  
  This parameter is crucial for stress testing and scenario analysis. A high \(p\) implies frequent, abrupt moves that are not captured by Gaussian models and indicates exposure to event risk, such as earnings announcements, regulatory changes, or macro shocks.

  \item \textbf{Jump mean \(\mu_J\): typical direction of extreme shocks.}  
  A negative \(\mu_J\) signals assets that are prone to downside crashes (e.g., broad market drawdowns), whereas a near-zero \(\mu_J\) reflects more symmetric jump risk. This is particularly important for identifying assets that contribute disproportionally to left-tail risk.

  \item \textbf{Jump volatility \(\sigma_J\): magnitude of extreme shocks.}  
  Larger \(\sigma_J\) indicates more severe tail behavior and fatter tails. This information can be used to distinguish assets with mild tail risk from those that experience truly extreme shocks, which is critical for designing jump-sensitive hedging and capital allocation rules.
\end{itemize}

Taken together, the jump-diffusion parameters provide a richer decomposition of risk than classical Gaussian models. Asset managers can use these estimates to:
\begin{itemize}
  \item adjust leverage and position sizes based on jump exposure,
  \item design hedging strategies that specifically target tail events,
  \item perform realistic stress tests using the estimated jump distribution,
  \item assess whether an asset's return profile aligns with a given risk budget,
  \item incorporate asymmetric jump risks into portfolio optimization and scenario analysis.
\end{itemize}

In summary, the real-data analysis confirms the practical relevance of jump-diffusion modeling: the estimated parameters offer actionable insight into tail risk, crash likelihood, and volatility regimes, all of which are central to modern risk management and portfolio construction.
